name: Lena Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What do you do on a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Lena, 58. I left secondary school and only moved from packing to running the label applicator at a household-cleaners plant this spring. I still ask the lead to check the first bottle after I change a roll; a crooked label can cover the safety instructions. I like seeing a full clean rack, but fishing torn backing paper out of the rollers makes me nervous.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home and money like, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Karim works changing hours as a security guard, and our grown children live on their own. I earn less than most operators here, we have about two weeks of expenses saved, and few similar plants are nearby. I have never used AI tools; I keep the label settings in a small notebook. Retirement is in sight as a question, but we have not seen figures that say we can afford to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say an office program can tidy the bottle orders, but the safety label still has to sit straight. I would keep asking the lead to check my first bottle after a roll change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be relieved if the label machine stayed familiar. The plant sometimes drops a paid packing shift when orders are slow, Karim's guard hours change, and two weeks saved does not absorb much. A quiet AI year does not make that small bank balance larger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the label applicator and checking the warning text on the first bottle. If the plant offers an extra paid Saturday, I would put a little of that newly earned pay aside after the food and heating bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about ordinary hours and bills, though the software itself does not frighten me. I sleep better when I know next week's rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What went wrong on a recent label change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week the backing paper tore and the warning strip slipped toward the bottle seam. The lead stopped me before I ran another rack, and we reset the roller together. A straight label can keep the warning from disappearing around a bottle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Saturday work is not offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then no extra money goes into the envelope that week. I will not move our two-week reserve around and call it new saving; the regular pay already has jobs to do.

say: I would say **safety labels** still need a person checking the first bottle.
The **lead check** matters after a torn roll even when orders are tidy.
think: My **low operator pay** and Karim's variable hours keep household money tight.
Two weeks of **savings** cannot cover a missing shift or large repair.
do: **Keep** running the label applicator and checking the first warning label.
**Save** a little from any offered paid Saturday after food and heating.
feel: **Anxious** about existing shift and bill pressure despite a familiar machine.
S0.quote: A straight label can keep the warning from disappearing around a bottle.
fieldNote: Lena is **new to the machine**, so a lead checks the first bottle after each roll change.
Her **baseline income risk** comes from variable paid shifts and guard hours; new saving requires offered extra pay.

steps.text: Keep running label applicator and checking first warning labels
Save part of newly paid Saturday wages after household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the plant AI might write orders and shift sheets first, while robots reach the bottle line more slowly. I would ask for the actual paid rota before anyone says a new camera needs one fewer operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the office shortens our changeover time, my junior shift could be the easiest to drop. Karim's guard rota cannot promise the difference, and two weeks saved is not enough for one missed wage. I am not ready to learn from a screen by myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the shift lead to compare the posted rota with my last three pay slips. If the factory requires camera-guard instruction and offers a paid supervised place on a stopped label machine, I would attend and practise the stop with the lead. If my regular hours are cut, I would apply for posted nearby packing or label jobs only where the duties are safe and base pay and travel cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a real cut to my hours. I can learn a guard from someone beside the machine, but I cannot learn my way out of an unpaid week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe instruction show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainer should have me isolate the rollers, clear a torn strip and restart on empty bottles. I would not put my fingers near moving backing paper because a video said it was safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take any nearby packing job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The posting needs a base wage we can live on and a bus time that gets me home after a full shift. I cannot pay for a longer journey on a lower rate.

say: I would ask for a **posted paid rota** before a camera reduces label staffing.
A **guard lesson** needs a stopped machine and a person teaching it.
think: My **junior shift** could disappear if changeovers are shortened.
Karim's **variable guard pay** and two weeks saved cannot replace it.
do: **Compare** posted label hours with three paid slips.
**Attend** required camera-guard training only if a paid stopped-machine supervised place is offered.
**Apply** after actual cuts only to posted safe nearby work at bill-covering pay and workable travel.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic paid-hour loss, while willing to learn beside the machine.
S1.quote: I cannot learn my way out of an unpaid week.
fieldNote: Her **training acceptance** is narrow: required, paid, supervised practice on a stopped machine, rather than self-study on AI.
A **job application** needs actual cut hours and posted safe work whose base pay and travel cover household bills.

steps.text: Compare posted label rota with last three pay slips
Attend guard course if required paid supervised stopped-machine place offered
Apply after cuts to posted safe nearby packing/label work if base pay and travel fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Karim that AGI could write factory orders by 2028, but capable robots that handle and label bottles arrive around 2031. I would ask the plant for written notice of which paid shifts are left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots can do the hands-on line work. I expect the newest operator shifts, including mine, to go first. Karim's changing guard wage and our two-week reserve cannot cover the household on their own, and I would lie awake trying to see where the next pay packet comes from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would cancel the paid television package and keep that money for food. If the plant offers a funded, paid practical course in bottle inspection with a trainer and guarded place, I would take it; after qualifying, if my label hours end, I would apply only to posted safe local inspection jobs with base pay and travel that cover our bills. Without a course seat I would search posted local packing work on the same terms while keeping any paid label shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the likely loss of my whole wage. A course is worth trying if it is real. A brochure cannot buy the next groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must an inspection course actually teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need to spot a missing warning word, stop the conveyor and check a test bottle with the trainer beside me. A printed certificate without guarded practice would not make me safe on a moving line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would retirement solve the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would get our actual pension and household figures before deciding when we can stop working. We have not shown that retirement pays for food and heating, so I would keep looking for paid work if the label shift ends.

say: I would separate **2028 order AGI** from capable bottle robots around 2031.
I would ask the plant for **written paid-shift notice** before cuts.
think: At **63**, I expect my junior label shift to be among the first lost.
Karim's changing wage and our **two-week reserve** cannot bridge a long gap.
do: **Cancel** paid television and keep the money for food.
**Take** funded paid guarded inspection instruction only if a real supervised place is offered.
**Apply** after lost hours to posted safe local inspection if qualified, or packing if no course, at bill-covering pay.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless pay-packet worry.
S2.quote: A brochure cannot buy the next groceries.
fieldNote: Her **age 63** is calculated at the 2031 physical robot date; the 2028 AGI change first touches orders.
She needs **actual paid instruction** and posted jobs, while retirement depends on figures she has not yet seen.

steps.text: Cancel paid television package to preserve food money
Take bottle-inspection course if funded paid guarded supervised place offered
Apply for posted safe local inspection if qualified and cut, base pay and travel fit
Search posted safe local packing if no course, base pay and travel fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the packers AGI may plan cleaner orders in 2031, while capable robots could handle the physical bottles around 2034. Five years gives people time to ask which paid jobs and lessons really exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 when robots reach the line. I might still need my wage then; I cannot guess what retirement would pay without the figures. If regular shifts continue, I could learn the inspection check in time, but a junior operator cannot buy a course with two weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the label shift and save a little new money from any offered paid extra day after bills. I would take the recognised bottle-inspection course only if the employer pays fees and release hours and offers guarded practice with a trainer. After passing, if my label hours fall, I would apply for posted safe local inspection work only if base pay and travel cover our bills; if no place opens, I would search posted packing work on the same pay and travel terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a longer warning lets me test a real offer while I still earn. I do not want to be sent home with only a certificate and no paid post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove the lesson worked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would reject a bottle with the warning printed under the seam and stop a test conveyor without touching the rollers. The trainer needs to see me do both before I am put on a live inspection shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a written estimate and compare it with our food, heating and housing costs. If the amount is short, I would plan to keep earning; I cannot build the budget from a birthday alone.

say: I would ask for **real paid places** before bottle robots reach the line around 2034.
The **2031 order change** is earlier than physical bottle handling.
think: At **66**, I may still need factory wages while retirement costs remain unclear.
A **funded lesson** could help only if a posted inspection job exists.
do: **Save** fresh pay from offered extra days after ordinary bills.
**Take** recognised inspection only with employer-paid fees, release and guarded trainer practice.
**Apply** after qualification and cuts to posted safe inspection, or packing without a course, at bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about later work and present thin savings, with time to verify terms.
S3.quote: I cannot build the budget from a birthday alone.
fieldNote: She makes no **retirement promise**: an estimate must be compared with real household costs before any decision.
Both **inspection and packing** routes need posted safe local work with base pay and travel she can afford.

steps.text: Save new wages from offered extra label days after bills
Take recognised inspection if fees and release paid and guarded trainer place offered
Apply for posted safe inspection if qualified and cut, base pay and travel fit
Search posted safe packing if no course, base pay and travel fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI could plan factory orders in 2036, while capable robots might label and pack bottles around 2039. A decade is a long time, but it does not turn a low wage into savings by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 71 when physical robots arrive, if I am still working then. Perhaps Karim and I can afford to stop before that, but I cannot assume it. Our two-week reserve and uncertain guard shifts make the present years worrying before the robot date matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working the label machine while it pays and ask for written pension and household cost figures this year. If an employer offers a paid, guarded bottle-check course with a trainer, I would take it only while I can still earn on my present shift. In the first year after 2036, if I am still employed and label hours fall, I would apply only for posted safe local packing or inspection work whose base pay and travel cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money now, although the robot date is far away. I will decide when to leave work from actual income, not from someone else's retirement calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make stopping work possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would need written pension figures and enough household income after food, heating and housing to last. If the sums do not work, I would keep looking for paid shifts rather than announce an exit date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could help you with the forms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown daughter can sit with us and read the figures, but I would not ask her to pay our bills. I want her help understanding the numbers, not an assumed second wage.

say: I would keep **2036 order AGI** separate from physical bottle robots around 2039.
A **long warning** does not settle today's household bills.
think: At **71**, I may or may not still need paid factory work.
Our **two-week cushion** and irregular guard hours make current money uncertain.
do: **Keep** paid label shifts and request written pension and household figures.
**Take** a guarded bottle-check course only if paid supervised practice protects current earnings.
**Apply** after 2036 cuts, if still employed, to posted safe local work at bill-covering pay and travel.
feel: **Anxious** about current money while leaving retirement timing open to actual figures.
S4.quote: I will decide when to leave work from actual income, not from someone else's retirement calendar.
fieldNote: A **retirement enquiry** is information gathering; she makes no exit commitment without written income and cost figures.
Training requires a **paid guarded place**, and any post-2036 search requires continued employment, cut hours and workable wages.

steps.text: Keep working paid label shifts while they remain
Request written pension estimate and household cost figures this year
Take bottle-check course only if paid guarded supervised place protects earnings
Apply after 2036 cuts if employed to posted safe local work if pay and travel fit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could remove my label shift before we know whether we can afford to stop work. Written paid-shift notice, an offered paid guarded lesson and posted safe local work at a usable wage would help. I would also need real retirement figures, not a guess about my age.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask about the warning label when a roll tears. A bottle may look fine on a pallet while its safety words have slipped into the seam. I want someone paid to stop that rack before it leaves.

headlineQuote: A bottle may look fine on a pallet while its safety words have slipped into the seam.
portrait: **Lena**, 58, is a junior label-machine operator who left school after secondary education and is still learning the equipment.
She and her **security-guard husband** Karim have grown children, variable household hours and about two weeks of expenses saved.
Her **low operator pay** and few nearby plants make ordinary wage changes anxious even before capable robots arrive.
She has **never used AI**, prefers supervised paid practical instruction, and will judge retirement from actual income and costs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable labelling robots around 2031 before she knows how to replace her wage.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **written shift notice**, paid guarded training, posted safe local work and real retirement-income figures.
